calib.source: 2020 -> 2024 change, final early vote vs presidential margin

notes.PA: No in-person early voting, so this is mail ballots returned. Pennsylvania's mail electorate is heavily Democratic whatever the year (about D+53 at 12 days out in 2022, when Republicans won the national House vote by 3), so it says little about direction; the slope fitted for mail-only states is small for that reason. Requests by party are shown for context.
notes.FL: Mail plus in-person. In-person early voting opens Oct 19 (Oct 24 in 2022, Oct 21 in 2024); until then this is mail only, and Florida Republicans moved toward mail after 2022. Florida's final early vote was R+6 in 2022 (result R+19) and R+9 in 2024 (result R+13).
notes.NV: Mail plus in-person, from the Secretary of State's daily files (UF Election Lab compiles them; Jon Ralston's blog reported the 2022 and 2024 leads used here). In-person opens Oct 17. 2022's early vote finished about D+1.5 and the Senate race was D+0.8; 2024's finished R+3.8 and the presidential race was R+3.1.
notes.CO: All-mail state; nearly every ballot is returned by mail or drop box. The Secretary of State posts a release each weekday from about three weeks out with returns by party; 2022 and 2024 points come from those spreadsheets.
notes.IA: Absentee ballots received, which in Iowa include ballots cast in person at the auditor's office. Iowa Democrats vote absentee far more than Republicans in every year (2022's absentee pool was D+19 while the Senate race was R+12), so the small mail-state slope applies. 2022 and 2024 points are the Secretary of State's daily reports as compiled by Bleeding Heartland.
notes.AZ: Early ballots returned, compiled from county reports by Stealth Analytics for UF Election Lab (Arizona has no official statewide daily file). No same-point baseline yet; the 2022 and 2024 final early votes are shown for context.

story.headline: North Carolina's first day of in-person voting was the most Democratic same-point reading yet: by the official files, 237,539 ballots had been accepted through Oct 15 against 189,375 at this point in 2022, with registered Democrats up from 79,117 to 111,482 and Republicans down from 54,195 to 46,341. Elsewhere the official comparison is still thin: Iowa's first 1,273 absentee ballots are D+44 against D+12 in 2022 (the pooled implied national margin, resting on Iowa alone, is D+4.4 with a ±4.2 band), Florida's mail vote was D+6.4 on Oct 15 with no 2024 match for that day, and Pennsylvania's, Nevada's and Colorado's baselines begin 12-15 days out. Georgia's in-person turnout is running 40% ahead of 2022's first day, but at the same days out its total early vote is 14% lower, because mail has collapsed and 2022's in-person voting opened a day earlier relative to Election Day.

story.compare_note: Democratic share of mail-ballot requests (CNN/Catalist, Oct 1). Gray dot is the same point in 2024. Virginia's early voters are 63% Democratic on L2's modeled two-party split, vs. 59% at the same point in 2024 (Morris, Oct 12); Ohio's early voters were 41% Democratic and 28% Republican by last primary ballot as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024 (News 5 Cleveland, from Secretary of State data). Florida's, Nevada's, Colorado's, Iowa's, Pennsylvania's and North Carolina's comparisons are computed from the official files; North Carolina's first in-person day (Oct 15) was 48% Democratic, 32% unaffiliated and 20% Republican by registration (Bitzer, Oct 16). CNN also found that the 2022 request pools were more Democratic than 2026's in every listed state except Iowa.

bullets.title: Georgia's in-person voting is 40% ahead of 2022, but its total early vote is not.
bullets.html: The Secretary of State counted 188,667 in-person voters on Oct 13, against 134,962 on the first day of 2022 and 70,849 in 2018, and more than 436,000 ballots had been cast by noon on Oct 15 (about 5.8% of active voters), with about 18,300 mail ballots accepted. Yet at the same days out GeorgiaVotes counts 380,948 ballots through Oct 14 against 443,696 in 2022, 14% fewer: 2022's in-person voting opened a day earlier relative to Election Day and its mail vote was several times larger. Through Oct 14, 53.6% of voters were 65 and over, 35.8% Black and 51.5% white; 78.6% had voted early in 2022.
sources: CBS News Atlanta (Secretary of State data), Oct 15
bullets.aff: Official data; GeorgiaVotes is an independent tracker of the state's files

bullets.title: North Carolina's first day in person was 47% ahead of 2022 and far more Democratic.
bullets.html: 201,609 in-person ballots on Oct 15 vs. 137,387 on 2022's first day (136,454 in 2018); nearly 96,000 from registered Democrats (48%, up 79% from 53,648), over 65,000 unaffiliated (32%, up 72%) and 40,105 Republicans (20%, down nearly 12% from 45,395). Mail is down 31% (35,932 accepted vs. nearly 52,000), so all early ballots are 25% ahead of the same point in 2022; two-thirds of day-one voters had voted in all four general elections since 2018, and 15% were under 45 (12% in 2022). The app's own comparison from the State Board's files (above) tracks the same point daily.
sources: NC State Board of Elections via the app's comparison, Oct 15

bullets.title: Ohio's early electorate has flipped from Republican to Democratic.
bullets.html: Democrats have returned about 94,000 ballots, unaffiliated voters a little more than 67,000 and Republicans nearly 64,000, by last primary ballot (Ohio Capital Journal, from Secretary of State data); News 5 Cleveland put Democrats at 41% and Republicans at 28% of nearly 230,000 early votes as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024. In-person votes in the first week were 194,841, nearly four times 2022's 50,368, and Cuyahoga, Lucas, Lorain and Summit counties have already passed 40% of their 2022 early-vote totals; but only 631,079 mail ballots have been requested vs. 871,041 at this point in 2022, and seniors are more than half of the ballots cast.
bullets.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet

bullets.title: The edge over 2024 is real but partly a change in how Democrats vote.
bullets.html: Democratic mail requests in North Carolina are down 40% from 2022, against 18% for Republicans, yet Democrats are returning ballots faster (22% returned vs. 17% in 2022). In Pennsylvania, 30% of the Democrats who had voted early by this point in 2024 have already voted again, vs. 18% of Republicans (L2 data via G. Elliott Morris). In an NBC poll, 23% of Democrats plan to vote by mail, down from 34% in 2024, and 36% plan to vote early in person, up from 30%.
bullets.aff: Nonpartisan; L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor

bullets.title: Wisconsin's mail vote is down 30% on 2022; Michigan's has flattened.
bullets.html: Wisconsin clerks had received about 128,000 absentee ballots three weeks out, against nearly 184,000 at the same point in 2022; Madison fell from about 31,700 to about 9,000, which Dane County's clerk attributes to distrust of the Postal Service. Michigan's returned absentee ballots (440,677 on Oct 13) are only slightly above the same point in 2022 (432,960), though requests are up more than 20% because of the permanent mail list. Neither state registers voters by party.

bullets.title: Florida's mail vote is a shade more Democratic than at this point in 2024.
bullets.html: By registration, 741,141 returned mail ballots were D+6.4 as of Oct 15 (316,330 Democrats, 268,675 Republicans, 156,136 others), down from D+6.7 a day earlier; the only matched 2024 point so far, Oct 14 (20 days out), was D+6.7 vs. D+5.8 in 2024. The 2024 baseline has gaps between 20 and 8 days out, so the app's card shows the comparison only on days it can match; the 2022 baseline begins at 18 days out (Oct 17). Republicans erased the Democratic mail lead once in-person voting opened in both 2022 and 2024; it opens Oct 19 this year, and about 1.59 million mail ballots are still out.
sources: Florida Division of Elections via the app's official comparison, Oct 15

bullets.title: Republicans say they vote later.
bullets.html: National Review's Noah Rothman argues Democrats will lead the early vote, "but perhaps not by the margins the party expects," because their own warnings eroded trust in mail. Ohio Republican strategist Bob Clegg says early voting "really tells you nothing" because Republicans vote later, while acknowledging a turnout problem. Wisconsin's GOP reads the Madison and Milwaukee declines as "a lack of enthusiasm among Dem voters." No quantitative RNC early-vote claims for 2026 turned up.
bullets.aff: GOP-aligned claims, reported by nonpartisan outlets

bullets.title: Nevada is the cautionary tale.
bullets.html: The Secretary of State's count doubled to about 30,000 ballots by the evening of Oct 15, almost 1.5% of active voters, all of it mail so far; Democrats lead by 7 points or more in three of the four congressional districts and trail by about a point in the 2nd, where Washoe County is 73% of the ballots and Democrats lead it by 8. That morning's count of about 14,500 had Democrats 1,260 ballots (9 points) ahead statewide. Jon Ralston says comparisons to past cycles are not useful yet. In-person voting starts Oct 17; in 2024 Democrats led the mail vote, Republicans led the total early vote, and Trump won.

story.calendar_note: North Carolina's one-stop voting opened Oct 15; Georgia's in-person voting opened Oct 13; Minnesota's statewide early voting on tabulators opened Oct 16; Iowa and Kansas mail ballots went out Oct 14. Colorado mailed its ballots Oct 2-9; Oct 19 is when its voter service centers must open. Pennsylvania and New Hampshire have no early in-person voting.
story.cast_at_note: Ballots counted (UF Election Lab, 39 jurisdictions reporting, state data as of Oct 9-16) when these comparisons were compiled; sets the automatic early-vote weight.
story.signals_verdict: The official same-point comparison leans Democratic where it exists but rests on little: North Carolina's day one by the state's files was far more Democratic by registration than 2022's (111,482 Democrats and 46,341 Republicans vs. 79,117 and 54,195), Iowa's 1,273 absentee ballots are D+44 vs. D+12 in 2022 and D+3.5 in 2024 (too few to mean much; the pooled implied national margin of D+4.4 ±4.2 is Iowa alone), and Florida's returned mail ballots were D+6.4 on Oct 15 with no 2024 point to match that day, in a state Republicans carried by 13. Everything else is more Democratic than 2024 wherever it can be measured, and against 2022 the picture is split: Georgia's and Ohio's in-person turnout is far ahead while mail is down in Wisconsin, Ohio and North Carolina, and Georgia's total early vote at the same days out is 14% below 2022; Democrats moving from mail to in person bends every comparison, so the early vote is consistent with the polls rather than ahead of them. The next tests are Nevada's in-person start on Oct 17, Florida's 2022 baseline (which begins at 18 days out) and its in-person start on Oct 19, and Colorado's first 2022 match on Oct 19.

signals.title: Georgia's in-person voting is running well ahead of 2022's pace
signals.value: 188,667 in-person votes on Oct 13 vs. 134,962 on the first day of 2022 (70,849 in 2018), per the Secretary of State; more than 436,000 ballots cast by noon on Oct 15, the third day, about 5.8% of active voters, with about 18,300 mail ballots accepted. Through Oct 14, 53.6% of voters were 65 and over and 35.8% Black (GeorgiaVotes).
signals.catch: Georgia has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction. Part of the in-person surge is voters who would have used mail, and at the same days out the total is below 2022 (see the other column); the 2024 first day was over 300,000.
signals.src: CBS News Atlanta (Secretary of State data), Oct 15; GeorgiaVotes, Oct 15
signals.aff: Official data via a nonpartisan outlet; GeorgiaVotes is an independent tracker of the state's files

signals.title: Ohio's early electorate has flipped from Republican to Democratic
signals.value: Democrats have returned about 94,000 ballots, unaffiliated voters a little more than 67,000 and Republicans nearly 64,000 (by last primary ballot), per the Ohio Capital Journal from Secretary of State data through Oct 12-13; News 5 Cleveland put Democrats at 41% and Republicans at 28% of nearly 230,000 early votes as of Oct 13, vs. 26% and 36% at this point in 2024. In-person votes after one week: 194,841 vs. 50,368 in 2022.
signals.catch: 2024 was a presidential year, and Ohio Republicans are shifting from mail to later voting: mail requests are 631,079 vs. 871,041 at this point in 2022. 'Party' is the last primary ballot pulled; seniors are more than half of ballots so far.
signals.src: Ohio Capital Journal (Ohio Secretary of State data), Oct 15; News 5 Cleveland, Oct 13

signals.title: Virginia's early voters lean further Democratic than in 2024
signals.value: 63% Democratic on L2's modeled two-party split, vs. 59% at the same point in 2024 (378,000 D to 265,000 R then). 46% of 2024's Democratic early voters have already voted again, vs. 35% of Republicans. CNN/Catalist (Oct 1): voters with only Democratic primary history lead those with only GOP history by 18 points, vs. 8 in 2024.
signals.catch: Virginia has no party registration, so party is modeled, and 2024 had a presidential-year electorate.
signals.src: G. Elliott Morris (L2 data), Oct 12; CNN/Catalist, Oct 1
signals.aff: L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor; Catalist is a Democratic-aligned vendor

signals.title: Democrats are returning their ballots faster than in 2022
signals.value: North Carolina: 22% of Democrats' requested ballots are back, vs. 17% at this point in 2022. Pennsylvania: 20% vs. 15%.
signals.catch: It could be enthusiasm, or worry that the mail will be slow; NBC/Penn say the data can't tell yet.

signals.title: Pennsylvania's 2024 Democratic early voters are coming back faster
signals.value: 30% of the Democrats who had voted early by this point in 2024 have already voted, vs. 18% of Republicans; of about 153,000 matched early voters, 76% are registered Democrats and 17% Republicans, vs. 66% and 25% at the same point in 2024.
signals.catch: L2's match covers less than half of the 346,932 ballots the state had counted by Oct 14; the official comparison (above) will supersede the party shares once the 2024 baseline reaches this point. Pennsylvania's mail vote is lopsidedly Democratic every year.
signals.aff: L2 is a nonpartisan commercial vendor

signals.title: Democrats' share of mail requests is up from 2024
signals.value: Iowa 67% vs. 54% at the same point in 2024; North Carolina 42% vs. 36%; Pennsylvania 66% vs. 62%; Maine 57% vs. 53%.
signals.catch: Against 2022 the same shares are lower everywhere except Iowa (see the other column).

signals.title: Trump country in New Jersey is voting less Republican
signals.value: In counties Trump won by 20+, the pre-election vote has shifted nearly 11 points toward Democrats vs. this point in 2024.
signals.catch: Small counties and a presidential-year baseline.

signals.title: Minnesota's accepted ballots are running 29% ahead of 2022
signals.value: 127,682 ballots accepted in the first three weeks of voting (through Oct 8: 47,968 in person, 79,714 by mail), vs. 99,252 at the same point in 2022; 468,860 ballots distributed vs. 405,721.
signals.catch: Minnesota has no party registration, so this is turnout, not direction, and its permanent absentee list has grown since 2022. Statewide early voting on tabulators only began Oct 16.

signals.title: At the same days out, Georgia's total early vote is 14% below 2022
signals.value: 380,948 ballots through Oct 14 (364,670 in person, 16,278 by mail), vs. 443,696 at this point in the 2022 general election, per GeorgiaVotes' reading of the state's voter file.
signals.catch: 2022's in-person voting opened a day earlier relative to Election Day (Oct 17, 2022 vs. Oct 13, 2026), so the 2022 figure carries one more in-person day, and 2022's mail vote was several times larger. Per in-person day, 2026 is well ahead; no party registration either way.
signals.aff: Independent tracker of the Secretary of State's voter file

signals.title: Wisconsin's mail vote is running 30% behind 2022
signals.value: About 128,000 absentee ballots returned three weeks out, vs. nearly 184,000 at the same point in 2022. Madison: about 9,000 vs. about 31,700.
signals.catch: No party registration; the Dane County clerk blames distrust of the Postal Service, and in-person absentee voting doesn't start until Oct 20.
signals.src: WPR, using Wisconsin Elections Commission data, Oct 13

signals.title: Michigan's mail returns have fallen back to the 2022 pace
signals.value: 440,677 ballots returned by Oct 13, vs. 432,960 at the same point in 2022; a week earlier returns were 30% ahead. Requests are up more than 20% (2,083,240 vs. 1,707,970).
signals.catch: Michigan has no party registration, so this measures turnout, not direction. About 95% of requests come from the permanent mail list; in-person early voting opens Oct 24.

signals.title: Against 2022, Democrats' share of mail requests is down
signals.value: Lower now than at this point in 2022 in every state CNN checked except Iowa.
signals.catch: Democrats are moving from mail to early in-person voting: 23% plan to vote by mail, down from 34% in 2024 (NBC poll).

sealed.note: SHA-256 fingerprints of the sealed versions of a separate, judgment-based forecast that is kept privately until after Election Day. Hash = SHA-256 of the version's full text (UTF-8) ending with one line break.

watch.note: Maintained daily. Every item links to the page that confirms it.
watch.trail_note: Trump and Vance campaign appearances since Sep 1, 2026, from White House pool reports, Roll Call Factbase and local coverage. Closed-press fundraisers and tele-rallies are rarely reported, so they are undercounted.

happened.title: Cook moves 11 more House races toward Democrats, half in Ohio, Nebraska and Kansas
happened.what: The Cook Political Report moved 11 House ratings, all toward Democrats, saying Republicans' troubles are 'particularly pronounced in Midwestern red states'; its Oct 16 ratings page lists the open MT-01 among 21 Toss Ups (16 Republican-held, 5 Democratic-held), MN-01, OH-10, OH-15, NY-21 and SC-01 as Lean Republican, and KS-02, NE-01 and FL-16 as Likely Republican.
happened.why: The House map keeps widening into Trump districts in states that also host competitive Senate races, so Republican money is being pulled in two directions.

happened.title: Musk is the donor behind SLF's $200 million Texas rescue
happened.what: Elon Musk gave Senate Leadership Fund $75 million on Sept. 9 and about $83 million two weeks later, money SLF routed into a 'Texas PAC' that has spent more than $159 million on ads for Ken Paxton and plans nearly $200 million, on top of $18.8 million from Musk's America PAC, mostly against James Talarico.
happened.why: Republicans are spending at a presidential scale to hold a Senate seat Trump carried by 14 points, money that is not going to Maine, Iowa, Ohio or Kansas.

happened.title: Democratic Senate candidates out-raise Republicans in every battleground
happened.what: Third-quarter reports: James Talarico raised $64 million to Ken Paxton's $18 million, Jon Ossoff $33.1 million to Mike Collins' $2.8 million, Abdul El-Sayed $30.7 million to Mike Rogers' $9.7 million, Sherrod Brown $23 million to Jon Husted's $5 million, Troy Jackson $20.4 million to Susan Collins' $5.2 million, Roy Cooper $20 million to Michael Whatley's $2 million, Mary Peltola $17 million to Dan Sullivan's $2 million, Josh Turek $12 million to Ashley Hinson's $3 million and Adam Hamilton $11 million to Roger Marshall's $800,000.
happened.why: Republican incumbents and nominees enter the final three weeks dependent on super PACs, whose ad rates are higher, in every seat that decides the Senate.

happened.title: Trump blames Cornyn and Rove in advance for any Paxton loss
happened.what: On Truth Social, Trump wrote that a Paxton defeat would be the fault of 'WEAK and INEFFECTIVE Political Hacks like John Cornyn and Karl Rove' and called James Talarico the 'antithesis of Texas values'; Cornyn has not endorsed Paxton and Rove has not said he will vote for him.
happened.why: The president is preparing an explanation for losing a Senate seat Republicans have held since 1961, four days before Texas early voting begins.

happened.title: Collins and Jackson close their debates with a shouted exchange
happened.what: In the fourth and final Maine Senate debate, in Bangor, a protester shouted about data centers, Sen. Susan Collins said he was 'obviously' from Troy Jackson's camp and Jackson told him to 'shut up'; Jackson said Collins votes with Trump 96% of the time, Collins put it at about 72%, and the moderator said the two have benefited from at least $75 million in dark money.
happened.why: Maine is a Republican-held seat every rater calls a Toss-up, and the exchange is being circulated by Senate Leadership Fund.

happened.title: Sullivan and Peltola accuse each other of lying in Alaska's Debate for the State
happened.what: Sen. Dan Sullivan said Mary Peltola's ads falsely tied him to Epstein-linked donors and asked whether she had the questions in advance (the hosts said no); Peltola said she cannot control PAC ads and called staff-abuse allegations against her 'outright fabrications or mass exaggerations.'
happened.why: Alaska is a Republican-held seat Inside Elections rates a Toss-up, and the debate came as both parties reserved more than $9 million each for the final three weeks.

happened.title: Justice Department sues to hold 20,000 California mail ballots
happened.what: The Justice Department sued California and two election officials, asking a court to block the counting of about 20,000 mail ballots from voters a federal list calls likely noncitizens until their citizenship is confirmed; similar lists in Nevada, Pennsylvania and New Jersey were found inaccurate, and Gov. Newsom called the suit an attempt to suppress votes.
happened.why: California holds several of the House seats that will decide the majority, and the suit tests whether federal list-matching can hold ballots after the 90-day limit on systematic roll maintenance.

happened.title: Republican Senate candidates break with Trump's Russian diesel deal
happened.what: Ashley Hinson, Dan Sullivan, Susan Collins, Jon Husted, Pete Ricketts, Mike Rogers and John Sununu have criticized or distanced themselves from the administration's deal to import Russian diesel, Collins signing a letter calling it 'a gift to our adversary'; Mike Collins, Roger Marshall, Darline Graham, Ken Paxton, Michael Whatley and Michele Tafoya have taken no position.
happened.why: Gasoline above $4 is the economic issue of the campaign, and the deal splits Republican candidates from the president in the states that decide the Senate.

happened.title: Sabato moves Kansas Senate to Toss-up, four other races shift
happened.what: Sabato's Crystal Ball moved Kansas from Leans Republican to Toss-up, citing 'a full-on Republican rescue operation' for Sen. Roger Marshall, and shifted Nebraska to Leans Republican, New Hampshire to Likely Democratic, Minnesota to Leans Democratic and Mississippi to Likely Republican.
happened.why: By Crystal Ball's count Republicans now need four of the five Toss-ups to hold the Senate while Democrats need two, the first time this cycle Republicans need more of them.

happened.title: Senate Majority PAC adds to Michigan and Maine, pauses Georgia and North Carolina
happened.what: Senate Majority PAC is adding $3.7 million in Michigan, bringing its total there to about $35 million, and $3 million in Maine, while pausing its ads in Georgia and North Carolina, where Jon Ossoff and Roy Cooper lead.
happened.why: Democrats' main Senate super PAC is treating Georgia and North Carolina as won and concentrating on the two Republican-held seats that would complete a net gain of four.

happened.title: GOP super PACs pull out of four House races, reinforce 16
happened.what: Congressional Leadership Fund canceled spending in IA-01, NJ-07, MI-08 and OH-01 and added money in 16 districts including PA-01, TX-15, WI-01, VA-01 and MI-04; a MAGA Inc. affiliate also pulled about $1 million meant to help Marty O'Donnell against Rep. Susie Lee in NV-03.
happened.why: House Republicans are conceding two of their own Trump-district seats and two Democratic targets to concentrate on districts Trump carried, narrowing their path to 218.

happened.title: Cook moves Alaska governor to Lean Democrat, three red states off Solid
happened.what: The Cook Political Report shifted the Alaska governor race from Toss Up to Lean Democrat, citing Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins' polling lead and a split Republican field, and moved Oklahoma, Nebraska and Vermont from Solid to Likely Republican.
happened.why: Cook says the shifts give Democrats a chance at a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010; its governor map now has four Toss Ups (Georgia, Nevada, Ohio, Wisconsin).

upcoming.title: Flanagan, Tafoya hold only Minnesota Senate debate
upcoming.what: Peggy Flanagan and Michele Tafoya debate at noon Central on MPR News' Politics Friday, moderated by Brian Bakst, on the radio and at mprnews.org.
upcoming.why: It is the only scheduled debate in a Democratic-held seat Inside Elections rates Lean Democrat, where Tafoya outraised Flanagan in the third quarter.

upcoming.title: Minnesota early voting on tabulators begins
upcoming.what: Minnesota's early voting period, in which ballots are fed directly into a counter, begins statewide and runs through Nov. 2; in-person absentee voting has been open since Sept. 18.
upcoming.why: Early votes begin in the Flanagan-Tafoya Senate race, which Inside Elections rates Lean Democrat, and in the MN-02 House race.
upcoming.src: Minnesota Secretary of State, accessed Oct 14

upcoming.title: Nevada early voting begins
upcoming.what: Early voting for the general election begins in Nevada and runs through Oct. 30.
upcoming.why: Early votes begin in Nevada's governor race and in House seats including NV-02, which Democrats recently added to their target list.

upcoming.title: Paxton's 'Come and Take It' bus tour begins in Rockwall
upcoming.what: Ken Paxton starts an 18-day, 30-plus-stop bus tour in Rockwall that is to end at the Alamo on Nov. 2.
upcoming.why: Paxton has accepted no debate, so the tour is his main in-person push in a Senate race rated a Toss-up.

upcoming.title: Texas early voting begins
upcoming.what: Early voting begins in Texas and runs through Oct. 30; the mail-ballot application deadline is Oct. 23.
upcoming.why: Ballots start banking in the Paxton-Talarico Senate race and a governor race Cook moved to Lean Republican on Oct. 1.

upcoming.title: Alaska and Colorado early in-person voting begins
upcoming.what: Early in-person voting opens in Alaska (through Nov. 3) and Colorado's voter service centers open (through Nov. 3); Texas also opens the same day.
upcoming.why: In-person ballots start in Alaska's Toss-up Senate race and Lean Democrat governor race and in Colorado's CO-08 Toss Up.

upcoming.title: Wisconsin in-person absentee voting begins
upcoming.what: Early in-person absentee voting begins in Wisconsin, with hours and locations set by municipal clerks.
upcoming.why: Early votes begin in the open Wisconsin governor race and in House battlegrounds such as WI-01.
upcoming.src: Wisconsin Examiner via News From The States, Sep 18

upcoming.title: Rogers, El-Sayed hold second Michigan Senate debate
upcoming.what: WXYZ-TV hosts the second debate between Republican Mike Rogers and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed at its Broadcast House studios in Detroit, airing statewide; no start time was listed.
upcoming.why: It comes three days before statewide early voting begins in Michigan.

upcoming.title: Marshall, Hamilton debate on Kansas Nexstar stations
upcoming.what: Sen. Roger Marshall and Democrat Adam Hamilton debate from 7 to 8 p.m. Central, originating at WDAF-TV in Kansas City and airing on Nexstar stations in Kansas City, Topeka, Wichita and Joplin.
upcoming.why: Cook rates the race a Toss Up, and both parties' main Senate super PACs are now spending on it.

upcoming.title: Crowley, Tiffany hold Wisconsin governor debate
upcoming.what: WISN-12 hosts a one-hour debate between Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany at Marquette University at 7 p.m. local time, also carried by partner stations in Green Bay, Madison, Wausau, Eau Claire and La Crosse.
upcoming.why: Tiffany has said one debate is sufficient, making this likely the only televised matchup in the open governor race.

upcoming.title: Sand, Lahn debate for Iowa governor
upcoming.what: Democrat Rob Sand and Republican Zach Lahn meet in a live 90-minute Iowa PBS debate at 7 p.m. Central.
upcoming.why: Iowa's open governorship is one of the competitive governor races.

upcoming.title: FEC pre-general reports due
upcoming.what: Pre-general reports covering Oct. 1 through Oct. 14 are due to the FEC.
upcoming.why: They provide the last full look at campaign and committee cash and spending before Election Day.

upcoming.title: Arizona mail-ballot request deadline
upcoming.what: Oct. 23 is the last day to request a mail ballot in Arizona; Oct. 27 is the last recommended day to mail it back, and in-person early voting ends Oct. 30.
upcoming.why: Arizona's governor race, rated Lean Democrat by Cook, and the AZ-01 and AZ-06 House seats are on the competitive list.

upcoming.title: Michigan statewide early voting begins
upcoming.what: Early in-person voting sites open statewide in Michigan, open at least eight hours a day through Nov. 1, with some communities offering extra days.
upcoming.why: Early votes start in the open Senate and governor races and in House battlegrounds such as MI-04 and MI-07.

upcoming.title: Florida mandatory early voting begins
upcoming.what: Florida's mandatory early voting period runs Oct. 24 through Oct. 31, and counties may offer additional days or hours.
upcoming.why: Early votes begin in the Senate race, a governor race Cook moved to Lean Republican, and House seats such as FL-13 and FL-27.

upcoming.title: Obama rallies in Cleveland and Detroit
upcoming.what: Former President Barack Obama is to campaign in Cleveland with Sherrod Brown and Amy Acton and in Detroit with Abdul El-Sayed and Jocelyn Benson on Oct. 24, the first Saturday of Michigan's statewide early voting; venues and times are to be announced.
upcoming.why: Ohio's Senate and governor races and Michigan's Senate race are Cook Toss Ups, and Trump and Vance have each campaigned in both states in October.

upcoming.title: Pennsylvania mail ballot application deadline
upcoming.what: Oct. 27 is the deadline to apply for a mail-in or absentee ballot in Pennsylvania, and completed ballots must reach county election offices by 8 p.m. on Nov. 3.
upcoming.why: Pennsylvania's House battlegrounds, including PA-01, PA-07 and PA-08, could help decide House control.
upcoming.src: Pennsylvania Department of State, accessed Oct 13

upcoming.title: Ohio absentee application deadline
upcoming.what: Absentee ballot applications must reach county boards by 8:30 p.m. on Oct. 27; early in-person voting runs extended hours Oct. 26-30, and mail ballots must arrive by 7:30 p.m. on Nov. 3.
upcoming.why: Ohio's Senate race between Jon Husted and Sherrod Brown and its open governor race are both Cook Toss Ups.
upcoming.src: Ohio Secretary of State, accessed Oct 14

upcoming.title: Maine no-excuse absentee voting period ends
upcoming.what: Oct. 29 is the last day of Maine's no-excuse absentee period, including in-person absentee voting at town and city halls.
upcoming.why: The deadline shapes early ballots in the Collins-Jackson Senate race and the ME-02 House race.

upcoming.title: Nevada polls close; Alaska follows after midnight ET
upcoming.what: Polls close at 10 p.m. ET in Nevada and Montana; most of Alaska closes at midnight ET and the Aleutian Islands at 1 a.m. ET on Nov. 4.
upcoming.why: Alaska's Senate race, rated a Toss-up by Inside Elections, is likely to be among the last competitive contests to report.

upcoming.title: First polls close in Indiana and Kentucky
upcoming.what: Polls in the Eastern time portions of Indiana and Kentucky close at 6 p.m. ET, with the rest of both states closing at 7 p.m. ET.
upcoming.why: The first returns of the night include House races such as KY-06, which Inside Elections moved to Lean Republican.

upcoming.title: Polls close in Georgia, South Carolina, Virginia, most of Florida
upcoming.what: Polls close at 7 p.m. ET in Georgia, South Carolina, Virginia and Vermont, in most of Florida (the western Panhandle at 8 p.m. ET) and at most New Hampshire polling places (all by 8 p.m. ET).
upcoming.why: First returns arrive in the Georgia, South Carolina, Florida and New Hampshire Senate races and the Georgia and Florida governor races.

upcoming.title: Polls close in North Carolina and Ohio
upcoming.what: Polls close at 7:30 p.m. ET in North Carolina, Ohio and West Virginia.
upcoming.why: Results begin in the North Carolina and Ohio Senate races and the Ohio governor race.

upcoming.title: Polls close in Maine, Pennsylvania, most of Michigan, Texas
upcoming.what: Polls close at 8 p.m. ET in Maine, Pennsylvania and the rest of New Hampshire, and in most of Michigan, Texas and Kansas, whose westernmost areas close at 9 p.m. ET.
upcoming.why: First results arrive in the Maine, Michigan, Texas and Kansas Senate races and the Michigan and Texas governor races.

upcoming.title: Polls close in Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, Wisconsin, Arizona
upcoming.what: Polls close at 9 p.m. ET in Iowa, Minnesota, Nebraska, Wisconsin and Arizona.
upcoming.why: Results begin in the Iowa, Minnesota and Nebraska Senate races and the Iowa, Wisconsin and Arizona governor races.

comps.note: Both states moved 9.0 points toward Democrats from 2024. The off-year governor races have pointed the right way before every midterm since 2006, with large misses in size.
